kaikki.etymology_text:
From Proto-Hellenic *tʰunkʰanō, from the nasal-infixed present *dʰu-n-gʰ- of Proto-Indo-European *dʰewgʰ- (“to hit, produce, yield”), whence also τεύχω (teúkhō, “produce”). The term is intransitive, though nasal-suffixes are otherwise generally associated with transitive-factitive semantics in Indo-European languages. According to the linguist Davide Bertocci, the sense "to achieve a goal, hit upon" has an implied object, which perhaps allowed for a reinterpretation as a telic verb and consequently the acquisition of nasal morphology. Compare ἱκάνω (hikánō, “to reach”).
The present stem τῠγχᾰ́νω (tŭnkhắnō) is a zero-grade form of the root with nasal infix and nasal suffix, like λᾰμβᾰ́νω (lămbắnō, “to take”) and λᾰνθᾰ́νω (lănthắnō, “to do secretly”). The aorist stem ἔτῠχον (étŭkhon) is zero-grade with no suffix, and ἐτῠ́χησᾰ (etŭ́khēsă), and τετῠ́χηκᾰ (tetŭ́khēkă) are zero-grade with regular first-aorist and perfect suffixes. The future τεύξομαι (teúxomai) and perfect τέτευχᾰ (téteukhă) and τέτευγμαι (téteugmai) are e-grade. Related to τεύχω (teúkhō), which is from a different present stem and with which it shares some forms.

kaikki.etymology_text:
The first component of the word is likely from Proto-Indo-European *pres (“before, in front”), an extended form of *per-. The second component is debated:
* From Proto-Indo-European *gʷṓws (“cattle”), thus "one who leads cattle".
* From Proto-Indo-European *gʷew-, a variant of *gʷem- (“to go”), thus "one who goes in front". Compare Sanskrit पुरोगव (purogava, “leader”), from पुरस् (puras, “in front”) and गम् (gam, “to go”).
* Together with the first component, from Proto-Indo-European *pre(y)sgʷu-, and cognate with Old Armenian երէց (erēcʻ, “elder, senior”) and Latin priscus (“ancient”), pristinus (“primitive, pristine”).

The first component of the word is likely from Proto-Indo-European *pres (“before, in front”), an extended form of *per-. The second component is debated:
* From Proto-Indo-European *gʷṓws (“cattle”), thus "one who leads cattle".
* From Proto-Indo-European *gʷew-, a variant of *gʷem- (“to go”), thus "one who goes in front". Compare Sanskrit पुरोगव (purogava, “leader”), from पुरस् (puras, “in front”) and गम् (gam, “to go”).
* Together with the first component, from Proto-Indo-European *pre(y)sgʷu-, and cognate with Old Armenian երէց (erēcʻ, “elder, senior”) and Latin priscus (“ancient”), pristinus (“primitive, pristine”).
